lead: A receiving antenna is the same metal as a transmitting antenna, used backwards. An incoming wave induces an open-circuit voltage, and a Thevenin source with the antenna impedance drives the receiver load. Reciprocity says the pattern, impedance and gain are the same in both roles, so one measurement serves both. Effective length and effective aperture turn a field strength or a power density into a received voltage or power. Link budgets, radar and RFID all use these ideas.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.3 for effective aperture and polarization, and Chapter 2.2 for directivity.

sections.h3: The receiving antenna as a Thevenin source

blocks.text: An incoming wave pushes charge along the metal. Model the antenna as a Thevenin source. E is the electric field strength in volts per metre (V/m). l<sub>eff</sub> is the effective length in metres (m). ψ is the angle between E and the antenna. The source sits in series with the antenna impedance Z<sub>a</sub> = R<sub>r</sub> + R<sub>L</sub> + jX<sub>a</sub>. R<sub>r</sub> is the radiation resistance; it represents power re-radiated. R<sub>L</sub> is the loss resistance; it represents heat. X<sub>a</sub> is the antenna reactance in ohms (Ω).

blocks.where: V<sub>oc</sub> is the open-circuit voltage in volts (V); E is the electric field strength in V/m; l<sub>eff</sub> is the effective length in m; ψ is the angle between E and the antenna.

blocks.text: Connect a load Z<sub>L</sub> = R<sub>load</sub> + jX<sub>load</sub>. R<sub>load</sub> is the load resistance in Ω. X<sub>load</sub> is the load reactance in Ω. I is the current in amperes (A), I = V<sub>oc</sub>/(Z<sub>a</sub> + Z<sub>L</sub>). The load power is P<sub>load</sub> = ½|I|²R<sub>load</sub>. Maximum power transfer needs a conjugate match, Z<sub>L</sub> = Z<sub>a</sub><sup>*</sup>, so R<sub>load</sub> = R<sub>r</sub> + R<sub>L</sub> and X<sub>load</sub> = −X<sub>a</sub>. Under this match the load gets the available power, the maximum power the source can deliver. For a lossless antenna an equal amount is scattered by R<sub>r</sub>. Half the captured power reaches the load, half is re-radiated; with loss, R<sub>L</sub> takes heat too.

Effective length converts field to open-circuit volts. Assume the current distribution is known. For a short dipole of physical length l much less than λ, with current falling linearly from the feed to zero at each end, leff = l/2. For an ideal Hertzian element of length l with uniform current, leff = l. For a half-wave dipole leff = λ/π ≈ 0.318λ. At 100 MHz λ = 3 m, so leff ≈ 0.955 m. Effective aperture converts power density to received power. For a polarization-matched, conjugate-matched lossless antenna, Pr = S Ae PLF. S is power density in W/m². Ae is effective aperture in m². PLF is the polarization loss factor from Chapter 2.3; it is 1 for matched polarization and 0 for cross-polarized. Ae = D λ²/(4π). D is directivity (dimensionless), λ is wavelength in m. A short dipole has D = 1.5. Ae is not the physical area of the wire. It can be much larger than the metal. At 100 MHz a short dipole has Ae = 1.5 × 3²/(4π) = 1.07 m², even though its metal area is tiny. Received power falls with λ² for fixed D, so small antennas capture little at low frequency. Use Pr in W; convert to dBm with 10 log₁₀(Pr/1 mW).

Reciprocity theorem: the transmit and receive patterns of an antenna are identical, and its impedance is the same in both roles. A two-way test makes this concrete. Use two identical antennas A and B, or at least antennas with equal radiation resistance, and terminate the receiver with the same load impedance in both measurements. Drive antenna A with current I and measure power P₁ at antenna B. Then drive B with the same current and measure at A. Under these conditions the received power is P₁ again. For identical antennas, the field at distance r is the same in both directions for the same current. Therefore one set of pattern or gain measurements describes both transmitting and receiving. This is why the Friis equation in Chapter 2.8 uses one gain for each end, and why a radar can use the same antenna to transmit and receive. Reciprocity also lets you find an unknown receiving antenna's gain by measuring it as a transmitter in a known setup.

figure.caption: Driving A and receiving on B gives P₁; swapping the roles gives P₁ again when the antennas are identical and the receiver load is the same. The equal powers are reciprocity.

messages.label: field E at the same r

spec.aria: A two-way timeline for identical antennas with the same load, showing that driving antenna A and receiving on B, then swapping the roles, gives the same received power, which is reciprocity.

examples.question: A short dipole of directivity 1.5 receives a wave at 100 MHz with power density S = 10 µW/m², polarization matched. Find its effective aperture and the power delivered to a matched load, in watts and dBm.
examples.check:
import math
c = 3.0e8
f = 100.0e6
D = 1.5
S = 10.0e-6
lam = c / f
Ae = D * lam**2 / (4.0 * math.pi)
Pr = S * Ae
Pdbm = 10.0 * math.log10(Pr / 1e-3)
print(round(lam, 3))
print(round(Ae, 3))
print(round(Pr, 8))
print(round(Pdbm, 2))

traps: A_e is not physical area. A thin wire can have A_e = 1.07 m² at 100 MHz while its metal area is tiny.
Conjugate match is Z_L = Z_a*, not Z_L = Z_a. Equal complex impedances do not give maximum power unless the reactances are already zero.
Under a conjugate match the load does not receive all intercepted power. For a lossless antenna half is scattered by R_r; loss resistance R_L adds heat.
Do not use physical length for a half-wave dipole's induced volts. l_eff = λ/π, not λ/2.
Forgetting PLF is a common slip. A cross-polarized wave gives zero received power even when A_e is large.

quiz.q: State the Thevenin model of a receiving antenna and define each impedance part.
quiz.a: A voltage source V_oc in series with Z_a = R_r + R_L + jX_a; R_r is radiation resistance, R_L is loss resistance, X_a is antenna reactance.

quiz.q: Why is a conjugate match used at the receiver terminals?
quiz.a: It makes R_load = R_r + R_L and cancels X_a, so the load receives the maximum available power from the Thevenin source.

quiz.q: A half-wave dipole receives at 300 MHz. Find l_eff.
quiz.a: λ = c/f = 1 m. l_eff = λ/π = 0.318 m.

quiz.q: A polarization-matched antenna with D = 2 at 1 GHz sees S = 1 mW/m². Find P_r.
Why can A_e exceed the physical area of a wire antenna?
quiz.a: A_e is a capture area set by directivity and λ², not by metal area. A thin resonant wire can capture power from a larger wavefront.

quiz.q: Reciprocity says patterns are identical. Why does that not mean transmit power equals receive power?
quiz.a: Reciprocity relates field and current ratios. Actual powers depend on the drive current, source and load. The same pattern only says relative response is unchanged.
The wave and antenna polarizations are orthogonal, so received power is zero even if A_e is large.

beyond: Not for the exam. In RFID and wireless power transfer, the same reciprocity argument sets how much DC power a tag can harvest from a reader field. In MIMO and massive MIMO, reciprocity is used to sound the uplink channel and reuse it for downlink beamforming, but the radio chains must be calibrated. Antenna noise and sensitivity are handled in Unit 5. Search terms: available power, equivalent circuit of receiving antenna, reciprocity calibration, polarization loss factor.
